a.title: A Happy Day to Remember the Dead
text: In Mexico, there is a special holiday called the Day of the Dead. It happens on November 1 and 2.
It is not a sad day. Families celebrate the people they loved who have died, with music, food, and bright colours.
Each family builds an altar at home. They put up photos, candles, flowers, and the favourite foods of the person who died.
Orange flowers called marigolds are everywhere. People believe their strong smell helps guide the spirits home.
You will see smiling skulls made of sugar, and faces painted to look like friendly skeletons.
The idea is beautiful: as long as we remember people, they are never truly gone.

b.title: Death as a Celebration
text: Each year on 1 and 2 November, Mexico fills with marigolds, music, and candlelight for the Day of the Dead — a holiday that treats death not with fear, but with warmth.
Its roots reach back thousands of years, to Aztec traditions that were later woven together with Catholic festivals. The result is uniquely Mexican.

At its heart is the ofrenda, a home altar decorated with photographs, candles, marigold flowers, and the departed's favourite food and drink. The living prepare it to welcome their relatives' spirits back for one night.
The imagery is famous worldwide: sugar skulls, elegant skeleton figures, and faces painted as beautiful calaveras. These are not meant to frighten, but to mock death gently and rob it of its terror.
Families gather in cemeteries too, cleaning graves and sharing stories late into the night, so that sorrow and laughter sit side by side.
The message is tender and bold at once: those we love are not lost while we still speak their names.

c.title: On Speaking Terms with Death
text: Most modern cultures keep death at arm's length, tidied into hospitals and hushed voices. Mexico's Day of the Dead takes the opposite path: for two days each November, it invites death to the party.

The festival is a graft of two traditions — ancient Mesoamerican beliefs about the cyclical nature of life and death, layered with the Catholic calendar brought by Spain. From this union grew something neither parent alone could have produced.

Its genius lies in tone. The ofrenda laden with marigolds and favourite foods, the grinning sugar skulls, the elegant skeleton known as Catrina in her fine hat — all treat the dead not as ghosts to be feared, but as guests to be welcomed, teased, and fed.

This is not a denial of grief; cemeteries on those nights are full of real tears. It is, rather, a refusal to let grief have the last word — a cultural insistence that love and memory outlast the body.
In a world that so often hides from mortality, the festival offers a quietly radical lesson: that we might live more freely, and love more fully, if we were a little less afraid of the end.

a.title: The First TV Station
text: Today, we can watch shows on TVs, phones and computers. But TV was once brand new.
On November 2, 1936, the BBC in London started the world's first regular TV service.
The pictures were black and white, and the screens were very small. Only a few hundred families in London had a TV set.
TV sets were very expensive, so many people watched in shops or at a friend's house.
In 1939, a big war started, and the BBC turned off its TV service. It came back in 1946.
From that small start, TV grew into something almost every home has today.

b.title: Switching On the World's First TV Service
text: On November 2, 1936, the BBC began broadcasting from Alexandra Palace, a hilltop building in north London. It was the world's first regular, high-definition public television service.
'High-definition' meant something very different then. Pictures were black and white, with a few hundred lines on screens no bigger than a book.

At first the BBC used two rival systems on alternate weeks: one designed by the Scottish inventor John Logie Baird and another by the company Marconi-EMI. The electronic Marconi-EMI system produced clearer pictures, and Baird's was dropped in 1937.

Television sets cost about as much as a small car, so only a few thousand households in the London area owned one. Viewers watched news, variety shows and coverage of events such as a royal coronation.
On September 1, 1939, as the Second World War approached, the service was switched off without warning. It returned in June 1946.
Within a few decades, television had become the centre of family life around the world.

c.title: Before Television Was Ordinary
text: Every technology that later becomes invisible begins as a spectacle. On November 2, 1936, the BBC opened the world's first regular 'high-definition' television service from Alexandra Palace in north London, and a handful of viewers peered at flickering black-and-white images on screens barely larger than a postcard.

The launch was also a contest. For several months the BBC alternated between John Logie Baird's partly mechanical system and the fully electronic one developed by Marconi-EMI. The electronic approach was sharper and more reliable, and by early 1937 Baird's pioneering equipment had been abandoned — a reminder that being first is no guarantee of winning.

Ownership was a luxury. Sets cost roughly as much as a modest car, and only a few thousand households could receive the signal. Yet those viewers glimpsed what was coming: live coverage that let ordinary people watch distant events as they happened.

The experiment was cut short on September 1, 1939, when the service went dark ahead of war; it resumed in 1946. Afterwards, television spread with astonishing speed, reshaping politics, advertising and family routines.
Looking back at 1936 is useful precisely because it makes television strange again — and invites us to ask which of today's expensive novelties will soon seem too ordinary to notice.

topic: The Earl Who Gave Us the Sandwich
zh: 三明治伯爵：一道點心的名字從哪來？
src: Smithsonian Magazine · BBC · The New York Times

a.title: Who Named the Sandwich?
text: November 3 is Sandwich Day in some countries. It is the birthday of a man from England called the Earl of Sandwich.
Long ago, people ate bread with meat or cheese. But it did not have a special name.
The story says the Earl was very busy. He did not want to stop and eat at a table.
So he asked for meat between two slices of bread. He could eat with one hand and keep working.
His friends liked the idea. They began to order 'the same as Sandwich'. Soon the food had a name!
Today, people all over the world eat sandwiches. In Taiwan, many students eat one for breakfast.

opts: Why the Earl of Sandwich was so busy
What people ate with bread long ago
Why students in Taiwan eat sandwiches
How the sandwich got its name

opts: He did not like eating with a fork

q.q: What did his friends begin to order?
opts: Meat with cheese

b.title: A Snack Named After an Earl
text: Americans celebrate National Sandwich Day on November 3, the birthday of John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who was born in England in 1718.
People had, of course, been eating bread with fillings for thousands of years. What Montagu gave the world was not the food itself but its name.

According to a popular story, first written down by a French visitor in the 1760s, the Earl was so absorbed in a long card game that he refused to leave the table and asked for beef between two slices of toast.
One of his biographers offers a less colourful explanation: Montagu, a hard-working politician who ran the navy, often ate at his desk while he worked.
Either way, the convenient snack became fashionable among his friends, who asked for 'the same as Sandwich', and the name stuck.
Today the idea has travelled everywhere, from Vietnamese bánh mì to Taiwan's gua bao — proof that a good idea can outlive the person it is named after.

q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第二項與文意相反。

c.title: How a Name Outlived a Man
text: Few aristocrats are remembered for their lunch. John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, born on November 3, 1718, held senior political posts and oversaw Britain's navy, yet his lasting fame rests on a convenient arrangement of bread and meat.

It is worth stressing that he invented nothing edible. Bread wrapped around fillings is ancient; what changed in eighteenth-century London was that a fashionable circle gave the habit a fashionable label.

The traditional explanation, recorded by a French travel writer in the 1760s, casts the Earl as a gambler too engrossed in cards to sit down for a meal. His modern biographer, however, finds the story implausible for a man of his workload and suggests a more mundane origin: meals snatched at his desk.
The disagreement is instructive. Colourful anecdotes travel faster than dull truths, especially when they flatter our assumptions about idle aristocrats.

Meanwhile the word escaped its origins entirely. Today 'sandwich' names countless variations, from Vietnamese bánh mì to Taiwanese gua bao, and has even become a verb. A forgotten politician survives as an everyday noun — a reminder that language, not achievement, often decides who is remembered.

a.title: Treasure Under the Sand
text: More than 3,000 years ago, a young king ruled Egypt. His name was Tutankhamun. He became king when he was only about nine years old.
He died young, at about 19. People put him in a tomb with many treasures.
Over time, sand covered the tomb, and people forgot about it.
On November 4, 1922, a British man named Howard Carter found a stone step in the sand. It led down to the tomb!
Inside, there were gold, jewels, chariots and a famous gold mask. There were more than 5,000 objects.
Many old tombs were robbed long ago. This one was almost full, so it taught us a lot about ancient Egypt.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The gold mask of a young king
The discovery of a young Egyptian king's tomb
How sand covered old tombs
Why many old tombs were robbed
q.why: 全文講圖坦卡門陵墓的發現；其他是細節。

q.q: How old was Tutankhamun when he became king?
opts: About nineteen
About three
About nine
About thirty
q.why: 第一段：about nine years old。十九歲是他過世的年紀。

opts: A stone step in the sand
The gold mask
A door full of treasure
The king's chariot

opts: a room full of gold
a king's palace
a hole in the sand
a place where a dead person is buried

q.q: Why was this tomb so important?
opts: It was almost full, so it showed us a lot about ancient Egypt
It was the biggest tomb in Egypt
It belonged to Egypt's most powerful king
It was the oldest tomb ever found

opts: It is the largest building in Egypt
It has the newest objects
It was easy to find
It kept more than 5,000 real objects together

gt.en: More than 3,000 years ago, a young king ruled Egypt.
gt.zh: 三千多年前，一位年輕的國王統治著埃及。

gt.zh: 人們把他和許多寶物一起放進一座陵墓裡。

gt.zh: 它一路通往陵墓！

b.title: Wonderful Things in the Valley of the Kings
text: On November 4, 1922, workers led by the British archaeologist Howard Carter uncovered a stone step in Egypt's Valley of the Kings, the desert burial ground of ancient pharaohs near the Nile.
Carter had searched the valley for years, funded by the wealthy Lord Carnarvon, and the money was running out. The step led to a sealed doorway — and to the tomb of Tutankhamun.
Tutankhamun became pharaoh as a child, around 1332 BC, and died at about 19. He was not an especially important ruler, which may explain why his small tomb was soon forgotten and buried under rubble.

That obscurity protected it. While most royal tombs had been looted in ancient times, Tutankhamun's still held more than 5,000 objects, including furniture, chariots, weapons and a solid gold mask weighing about ten kilograms.
Carter's team spent around ten years carefully recording and removing everything.
When Lord Carnarvon died a few months after the opening, newspapers spread rumours of a 'pharaoh's curse'. Scientists point out that most people who entered the tomb lived long, ordinary lives.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Tutankhamun was a powerful king, so his tomb was full of treasure.
Because it was forgotten, Tutankhamun's tomb survived almost untouched, and its 1922 discovery revealed thousands of treasures.
Lord Carnarvon died because of a pharaoh's curse.
Carter searched the Valley of the Kings for many years.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第二項因果錯誤（他並不重要）；第三項是謠言。

q.q: Who paid for Carter's search?
opts: The Egyptian government
A British museum
Lord Carnarvon
Carter himself
q.why: 第二段：funded by the wealthy Lord Carnarvon。

q.q: About how much does the gold mask weigh?
opts: About ten kilograms
About one kilogram
About fifty kilograms
About one hundred kilograms
q.why: 第四段：about ten kilograms。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “looted” means ___.
opts: carefully studied
covered with sand
moved to a museum
robbed of valuable things
q.why: looted = 被洗劫。

q.q: What does the writer think about the 'pharaoh's curse'?
opts: It was a newspaper rumour, not supported by the facts
It is partly true because Carnarvon died
Scientists are still unsure
It is the reason the tomb was forgotten
q.why: 最後一段：most people who entered the tomb lived long, ordinary lives。

q.q: A video claims: “Everyone who entered the tomb died young because of the curse.” Which fact from the text best challenges this claim?
opts: Carnarvon died a few months after the opening
The tomb was full of gold
Carter worked for about ten years
Most people who entered the tomb lived long, ordinary lives
q.why: 大多數進入陵墓的人都活得很長，直接反駁這個說法。

tr.en: Carter had searched the valley for years, funded by the wealthy Lord Carnarvon, and the money was running out.
tr.zh: 卡特在富有的卡那封勳爵資助下，已經在山谷裡找了好幾年，而經費快要用完了。

tr.en: Tutankhamun became pharaoh as a child, around 1332 BC, and died at about 19.
tr.zh: 圖坦卡門在大約西元前 1332 年還是個孩子時就成了法老，大約十九歲就過世了。

tr.en: When Lord Carnarvon died a few months after the opening, newspapers spread rumours of a 'pharaoh's curse'.
tr.zh: 陵墓開啟幾個月後卡那封勳爵過世，報紙就散播起「法老的詛咒」的謠言。

c.title: The Advantage of Being Forgotten
text: History usually rewards the powerful with remembrance. Tutankhamun's posthumous fame is a rare exception: he became the most famous pharaoh of all precisely because his own civilisation forgot him.

Crowned as a child around 1332 BC and dead by about nineteen, he ruled during an unsettled period and left little political mark. His modest tomb in the Valley of the Kings was soon buried under debris from later construction, slipping from memory while grander tombs nearby were systematically plundered.

On November 4, 1922, after years of fruitless digging financed by Lord Carnarvon, Howard Carter's workmen exposed a step cut into the rock. Behind the sealed doors lay a near-intact royal burial: more than 5,000 objects, from gilded shrines and chariots to the gold mask that has become a global emblem of ancient Egypt.

The discovery also produced a modern myth. Carnarvon's death months later, from an infected mosquito bite, fed press stories of a vengeful curse — a tale that sold newspapers far better than painstaking archaeology ever could.
Perhaps the deeper lesson concerns what survives. The objects that tell us most about the past are often those that escaped attention, not those that commanded it.
gloss: 費盡心力的；一絲不苟的

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Tutankhamun became famous because his tomb was forgotten and therefore survived intact.
Tutankhamun was famous because he was a great ruler.
The curse made Tutankhamun famous.
Carter was the most important archaeologist in history.
q.why: 主旨：被遺忘反而讓陵墓完整保存，他也因此成名。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “posthumous” fame is fame that comes ___.

because of wealth
from political power

q.q: Why does the writer say the curse story “sold newspapers far better than painstaking archaeology”?

Because the curse was proven true
Because readers prefer dramatic stories to slow, careful science
Because newspapers paid for the excavation
q.why: 聳動的詛咒故事比嚴謹考古更吸引讀者。

q.q: What is the writer's attitude to the 'curse'?
opts: Fearful
Neutral and undecided
Amused but convinced
Sceptical
q.why: 稱其為 modern myth 並指出真正死因。

q.q: How does the essay's ending relate to its opening?
opts: It contradicts the opening
It repeats the list of treasures
It introduces Carter's later life
It widens the opening paradox into a general lesson about what survives from the past
q.why: 開頭的悖論在結尾延伸為普遍啟示。

q.q: According to the writer's final idea, which kind of object is MOST likely to teach future historians about everyday life today?

Statues of presidents

Gold medals from the Olympics
q.why: 結尾：最能告訴我們過去的，常是沒被注意的東西。

a.title: Run to High Ground!
text: November 5 is World Tsunami Awareness Day. A tsunami is a group of very big, strong waves.
Most tsunamis happen after a big earthquake under the sea. The water moves, and huge waves rush to the coast.
There are warning signs. The ground may shake hard. Sometimes the sea goes far away from the beach very quickly.
If you see these signs near the sea, do not stay to look. Run to high ground right away!
The day comes from an old story in Japan. A man burned his rice to call villagers up a hill, and they were saved from a tsunami.
Taiwan is next to the sea, so it is important for everyone to know what to do.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: What a tsunami is and how to stay safe
An old Japanese story about burning rice
Why Taiwan is next to the sea
How earthquakes happen under the sea

q.q: What usually causes a tsunami?

Heavy rain for many days
A full moon
A big earthquake under the sea
q.why: 第二段：after a big earthquake under the sea。

opts: Go to the beach to look at the sea
Run to high ground right away
Wait for an official alarm first
Stay inside a house near the beach

a high hill
the land next to the sea
a big wave

Because the rice was wet from the waves

gt.en: November 5 is World Tsunami Awareness Day.

gt.en: A man burned his rice to call villagers up a hill, and they were saved from a tsunami.
gt.zh: 一個男人燒掉自己的稻子，把村民召到山丘上，他們因此逃過了海嘯。

b.title: Knowing the Signs Saves Lives
text: Every November 5, the United Nations marks World Tsunami Awareness Day. It was created in 2015 to help people around the world understand one of nature's most destructive hazards.

Tsunamis are usually triggered by powerful undersea earthquakes, which suddenly lift or drop huge areas of the sea floor. The waves can cross an ocean at the speed of a jet plane and grow much taller as they reach shallow water.
History shows how deadly they can be. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed around 230,000 people in more than a dozen countries, and in 2011 a tsunami devastated Japan's northeast coast.

Yet many deaths can be prevented. Natural warnings include strong or long shaking, a loud roar from the ocean, and the sea suddenly pulling back from the shore. Anyone who notices them should head inland or uphill immediately, without waiting for an official alarm.
The date honours a Japanese story from 1854, in which a villager set fire to his harvested rice to lead people to safety.
Taiwan, surrounded by sea and sitting on active fault lines, runs warning systems and drills — but personal knowledge is still the fastest alarm.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Tsunamis are deadly, but knowing their natural warning signs and acting quickly can save many lives.
The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed around 230,000 people.
Tsunami waves can cross an ocean as fast as a jet plane.
Official warning systems make personal knowledge unnecessary.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第四項與文意相反。

q.q: How fast can tsunami waves cross an ocean?
opts: As fast as a car on a highway
As fast as a jet plane
As slowly as a ship
As fast as sound
q.why: 第二段：at the speed of a jet plane。

q.q: Which is NOT listed as a natural warning sign?
opts: Strong or long shaking
A loud roar from the ocean
Dark clouds and heavy rain
The sea suddenly pulling back
q.why: 第四段列出搖晃、轟鳴、海水急退；沒有提到烏雲大雨。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “inland” means ___.
opts: along the beach
onto a boat
into a tall building by the sea
away from the coast, towards the middle of the land
q.why: inland = 往內陸。

q.q: Why does the writer say personal knowledge is “the fastest alarm”?
opts: People can act the moment they notice the signs, before an official warning arrives
Official alarms do not exist in most places
Phones always fail during earthquakes
Personal knowledge is more accurate than science
q.why: 看到徵兆就能立刻行動，不必等官方警報。

q.q: Your school is planning a tsunami drill. Which plan matches the text's advice best?

Practise going to the beach to check the water

tr.en: It was created in 2015 to help people around the world understand one of nature's most destructive hazards.
tr.zh: 它在 2015 年設立，目的是幫助世界各地的人了解大自然最具破壞力的災害之一。

tr.en: Tsunamis are usually triggered by powerful undersea earthquakes, which suddenly lift or drop huge areas of the sea floor.
tr.zh: 海嘯通常是由強烈的海底地震引發的，這種地震會突然抬升或下沉大片的海床。

tr.en: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed around 230,000 people in more than a dozen countries, and in 2011 a tsunami devastated Japan's northeast coast.
tr.zh: 2004 年的印度洋海嘯在十幾個國家奪走了大約二十三萬人的性命，而 2011 年的一場海嘯則重創了日本的東北海岸。

c.title: The Ten Minutes That Matter
text: Tsunamis compress catastrophe into a cruelly short window. When a large undersea earthquake abruptly displaces the sea floor, waves can race across an ocean at jet-like speeds, then rear up as they meet shallow coastal water. Communities nearest the epicentre may have only minutes.

World Tsunami Awareness Day, adopted by the United Nations in 2015 and marked on November 5, exists because those minutes are where lives are won or lost. The 2004 Indian Ocean disaster, which killed roughly 230,000 people, exposed how few coastal residents recognised the danger signs or had anywhere planned to go.

The date commemorates the Japanese legend of 'Inamura-no-hi', in which, after an 1854 earthquake, a villager set his own harvested rice sheaves alight to draw neighbours uphill before the sea struck. The story endures because its logic is timeless: act decisively on the evidence in front of you, even at personal cost.

Modern warning networks, Taiwan's included, have improved dramatically, yet they cannot entirely replace instinct. Strong shaking, a sudden retreat of the sea or an unfamiliar roar should trigger evacuation on their own.
Preparedness, in the end, is less a technology than a habit — one that must be learned long before the water arrives.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?

Tsunamis are rare, so preparation is not necessary.
Because tsunamis give little warning, survival depends on people recognising the signs and acting at once — a habit that must be learned in advance.
The Inamura-no-hi story is the main reason the day exists.
q.why: 主旨：預警時間極短，存活靠事先養成的習慣。

q.q: Why does the writer say the Inamura-no-hi story's logic is “timeless”?

Because the story is very old
Because Japan still burns rice as a warning
Because acting quickly on the evidence, even at personal cost, is always the right response
q.why: 第三段：act decisively on the evidence … even at personal cost。

q.q: What is the writer's tone?
opts: Calm and relaxed
Urgent but practical
Hopeless
Angry at governments
q.why: 強調分秒必爭，又給具體做法。

To describe Taiwan's coast
q.why: 結尾收束：防災是習慣。

a.title: The Monkey Born from a Stone
text: A long time ago, in a Chinese story, a monkey was born from a magic stone. His name was Sun Wukong, the Monkey King.
He was very clever and very strong. He learned 72 ways to change his shape, and he could jump onto a cloud and fly far away.
He had a magic stick. It could become as small as a needle or as big as a tree.
But the Monkey King was proud and naughty. He made a lot of trouble in Heaven, so the Buddha trapped him under a mountain.
Five hundred years later, a kind monk freed him. The Monkey King promised to protect the monk on a long trip to the West.
Today, children all over the world know the Monkey King from books, cartoons and games.

b.title: From Troublemaker to Protector
text: Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, is the star of Journey to the West, a sixteenth-century Chinese novel usually credited to Wu Cheng'en. It remains one of the most beloved stories in Asia.

Born from a stone on a mountaintop, Wukong becomes king of the monkeys and then sets out to find the secret of eternal life. He masters 72 transformations, can travel 108,000 li in a single somersault, and wields a staff that can shrink to the size of a needle.
Power goes to his head. He declares himself 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven', steals heavenly peaches and fights off entire armies of gods, until the Buddha traps him under a mountain.

Five centuries later, the monk Tang Sanzang releases him on condition that he guards the monk on a dangerous pilgrimage to India to collect Buddhist scriptures. A golden band around Wukong's head tightens whenever he disobeys.
Along with Pigsy and Sandy, he battles demons through eighty-one trials.
The story still inspires films, comics and video games, including the hit game Black Myth: Wukong.

opts: The Monkey King can change into 72 different shapes.

Black Myth: Wukong is a hit video game.
In Journey to the West, the powerful but rebellious Monkey King is punished and then becomes a protector on a long pilgrimage.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是細節。

q.q: What title did Wukong give himself?

King of the Monkeys
Protector of the Monk
Master of 72 Transformations
q.why: 第三段：'Great Sage Equal to Heaven'。

q.q: What happens when Wukong disobeys?
opts: His staff shrinks to the size of a needle
He is sent back under the mountain
The golden band around his head tightens

q.q: In paragraph 4, a “pilgrimage” is ___.

a journey to a holy place
a punishment from the gods
a royal ceremony

q.q: What does “Power goes to his head” mean?

He becomes wiser as he grows stronger

q.q: Which modern situation is most like the golden band on Wukong's head?

tr.zh: 美猴王孫悟空是《西遊記》的主角，這是一部十六世紀的中國小說，一般認為作者是吳承恩。

tr.en: Born from a stone on a mountaintop, Wukong becomes king of the monkeys and then sets out to find the secret of eternal life.

tr.zh: 每當悟空不聽話，他頭上的金箍就會收緊。

c.title: Why We Love a Rebel Who Learns
text: Few literary characters have proved as durable as Sun Wukong. The Monkey King of Journey to the West, the sixteenth-century Ming novel traditionally attributed to Wu Cheng'en, has leapt from woodblock prints to opera stages, cartoons and blockbuster video games.

His appeal begins with his outrageous abilities: born from stone, he commands 72 transformations, crosses impossible distances in a single cloud somersault and wields a staff that expands or shrinks at will. Yet the novel is less interested in power than in what power does to character.

Intoxicated by his talents, Wukong proclaims himself 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven' and turns the celestial court upside down, until the Buddha pins him beneath a mountain for five hundred years. Freed to escort the monk Tang Sanzang to India in search of scriptures, he is fitted with a golden headband that tightens when he strays — a vivid image of discipline imposed from outside.
Over eighty-one ordeals, the trickster gradually becomes a loyal guardian, his brilliance redirected rather than extinguished.
That arc may explain his staying power. Wukong flatters our rebellious instincts while reassuring us that cleverness, properly harnessed, can serve something larger than oneself.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Wukong is popular only because of his magic powers.
Wukong endures because his story shows a brilliant rebel learning to direct his talents toward a larger purpose.
Wukong's story shows that rebels must lose their talents to become good.
Journey to the West is mainly a story about the monk.
q.why: 主旨：天才叛逆者學會把才能用在更大的目標。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “ordeals” are ___.
opts: magic transformations
long speeches

b.title: Two Nobel Prizes and a Notebook That Still Glows
text: Maria Skłodowska was born in Warsaw on November 7, 1867. Because women could not attend university in Russian-ruled Poland, she studied in secret before moving to Paris in 1891, where she enrolled at the Sorbonne.
There she met the physicist Pierre Curie, and the couple began investigating the mysterious rays given off by uranium. Marie coined the word 'radioactivity' to describe them.
In 1898 they announced two new elements: polonium, named after her homeland, and radium. Isolating them meant processing tonnes of mineral waste in a leaky shed.

In 1903 Marie became the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, shared with Pierre and Henri Becquerel. After Pierre died in a street accident in 1906, she took over his professorship and won a second Nobel, in chemistry, in 1911 — still the only person honoured in two different sciences.
During the First World War she equipped vehicles with X-ray machines to help army surgeons.
She died in 1934 from illness linked to years of radiation exposure. Her notebooks remain so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes.

c.title: The Price of Discovery
text: Marie Curie's biography reads like a sequence of barriers overcome. Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw on November 7, 1867, she grew up under Russian rule in a society that excluded women from higher education, and studied clandestinely before reaching Paris and the Sorbonne in 1891.

With her husband Pierre, she pursued the strange emissions of uranium, coining the term 'radioactivity' and, in 1898, announcing two new elements: polonium, a pointed tribute to her occupied homeland, and radium. Extracting even tiny quantities required years of gruelling labour in a draughty shed.

Recognition came, though not without resistance. She became the first woman Nobel laureate in 1903, and after Pierre's sudden death she won a second prize, in chemistry, in 1911 — a distinction no one has matched across two sciences. Yet the French press also hounded her over her private life, and a scientific academy rejected her membership.

Her legacy is double-edged. Radioactivity transformed medicine and physics, and during the First World War her mobile X-ray units aided countless wounded soldiers. But the hazards were poorly understood: she died in 1934 of a condition linked to prolonged exposure, and her papers still require protective handling.
Curie's life thus embodies both the brilliance of science and the cost of discovering something before we know how dangerous it is.

b.title: Lamps Against the Dark
text: Diwali, which falls on November 8 this year, is one of the most important festivals in India, celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains as well as by communities from Singapore to Britain.

Its name comes from a Sanskrit word meaning 'row of lights'. Families place rows of small clay oil lamps, called diyas, along windows, roofs and doorways, and many cities glow with electric decorations.

Different traditions explain the festival in different ways. In much of northern India, Diwali marks the return of the prince Rama to his kingdom of Ayodhya after defeating the demon king Ravana; people lit lamps to guide him home.

Many families also pray to Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and good fortune, after cleaning and decorating their homes. Rangoli — bright patterns made from coloured powder, rice or flowers — welcome guests at the door.
The celebrations usually last five days and are filled with family visits, gifts and sweets.
In recent years, some cities, including Delhi, have limited fireworks because of serious air pollution, encouraging quieter, greener ways to celebrate.

c.title: A Festival of Many Meanings
text: Diwali, which in 2026 falls on November 8, is often summarised as India's 'festival of lights', a phrase that captures its spectacle but understates its variety. Celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, and by diaspora communities across the globe, it carries different stories for different people.

In northern India it commemorates the homecoming of Rama to Ayodhya after his victory over the demon king Ravana; elsewhere it honours Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, or marks other religious milestones. What unites these traditions is a shared symbolism: light dispelling darkness, knowledge overcoming ignorance.

The rituals are tangible and communal. Homes are scrubbed and adorned, rows of clay diyas flicker on balconies, and intricate rangoli patterns welcome visitors. Over five days, families exchange sweets and gifts, settle accounts and renew relationships.

Modernity has complicated the picture. Fireworks, long central to the celebrations, now contribute to hazardous smog in cities such as Delhi, prompting bans and debates about whether tradition must bend to public health.
Diwali thus offers a vivid example of how a living festival evolves: its core meaning endures while its practices are continually renegotiated by each generation.

b.title: Halfway Through, Voters Have Their Say
text: On Tuesday, November 3, Americans head to the polls for the 2026 midterm elections. By law, federal elections are held on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

Midterms take place halfway through a president's four-year term. The presidency itself is not on the ballot, but voters decide who will sit in Congress, the branch of government that writes laws and controls federal spending.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for election, because House members serve two-year terms. Senators serve six-year terms, so only about a third of the 100 Senate seats are contested this year. Most states are also electing governors, along with thousands of local officials.

Going into the vote, Republicans held narrow majorities in both chambers. Historically, the president's party has usually lost seats in midterm elections, partly because voters often use them to express how they feel about the government's performance.
Results can take days in close races, as mail-in ballots are counted.

c.title: A National Report Card
text: Every two years, American politics pauses for a verdict, and the 2026 midterm elections on November 3 are the latest. Falling midway through a presidential term, they leave the White House untouched but decide who controls Congress — and therefore how much of a president's agenda can survive the remaining two years.

The mechanics explain the stakes. All 435 members of the House of Representatives face voters, since they serve two-year terms, while roughly a third of the Senate's 100 seats rotate on six-year cycles. Dozens of governorships and thousands of state and local offices are decided on the same ballot.

Political scientists often describe midterms as a referendum on the incumbent. The president's party has lost ground in most midterms of the modern era, a pattern attributed to voters' tendency to check whoever holds power and to the lower turnout of more satisfied supporters.

Going into the vote, Republicans held slim majorities in both chambers, so even a modest shift could transfer control and usher in a period of divided government — gridlock to some, healthy restraint to others.
Whatever the outcome, the midterms illustrate a defining feature of the American system: power is deliberately fragmented, and voters are given frequent chances to rebalance it.
gloss: 公投；（對施政的）信任投票

q.q: Which best captures the writer's point?
opts: Midterms decide which party chooses the next president.
Midterms act as a frequent check on power, deciding control of Congress and how much of the president's agenda can continue.
Midterms are less important than presidential elections.
Divided government always leads to gridlock.
q.why: 主旨：期中選舉是對權力的定期檢驗。

q.q: In paragraph 3, the “incumbent” is ___.
opts: the person or party currently in power
the party that lost the last election
a new candidate
a voter who supports the president
q.why: incumbent = 現任者。

q.q: Why might the president's party tend to lose seats in midterms, according to the text?
opts: The president's supporters always vote more in midterms
The law limits the president's party
Midterm ballots are harder to understand
Voters often want to check whoever holds power, and satisfied supporters vote less
q.why: 第三段。

q.q: How does the writer describe divided government?
opts: As always harmful
As always healthy
In a balanced way — 'gridlock to some, healthy restraint to others'
As illegal
q.why: 第四段。

q.q: What idea does the final paragraph highlight?
opts: That the president should have more power
That midterms should be cancelled
That the Senate is more important than the House
That the American system deliberately spreads out power and lets voters rebalance it frequently
q.why: 結尾。

q.q: Taiwan also holds elections at different times for different offices. Which statement best applies the writer's idea to Taiwan?
opts: Frequent elections give voters regular chances to check and rebalance those in power
Elections should be held only once every ten years
Only one office should be elected
Elections never change anything
q.why: 作者強調頻繁選舉讓選民有機會再平衡權力。

discuss: Why do you think the US holds elections for Congress every two years instead of only when choosing a president?
Compare elections in the US and in Taiwan. What is similar and what is different?
Some people think 'divided government' slows things down; others think it stops one side from having too much power. Which view do you agree with, and why?

topic: Carl Sagan and the Pale Blue Dot
zh: 卡爾・薩根與「暗淡藍點」
src: NASA · Science · The New York Times

a.title: A Tiny Blue Dot in Space
text: Carl Sagan was born on November 9, 1934, in New York. He loved the stars when he was a child.
He grew up to be a scientist who studied planets.
He also made a famous TV show called Cosmos. It helped millions of people learn about space.
In 1990, a spacecraft called Voyager 1 was very far from home. Sagan asked NASA to turn its camera and take a photo of Earth.
In the photo, Earth looks like a very small blue dot. People call it the Pale Blue Dot.
Sagan said the photo shows that our planet is small and special, so we must take care of it and of each other.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How Carl Sagan made the TV show Cosmos
Carl Sagan's life and a famous photo that shows how small Earth is
How Voyager 1 travelled far away from Earth
Why NASA took photos of other planets
q.why: 全文以薩根為主，重點是他請 NASA 拍的地球照片與其意義；其他選項只是文中細節。

q.q: What was Cosmos?
opts: A spacecraft that took a photo of Earth
The name of the photo of Earth
A TV show that helped people learn about space
A planet that Sagan studied
q.why: 第三段：a famous TV show called Cosmos。

q.q: Who asked NASA to take the photo of Earth?
opts: Carl Sagan
Voyager 1's team, to test the camera
Millions of TV viewers
NASA's leaders, for a TV show
q.why: 第四段：Sagan asked NASA to turn its camera。

q.q: In the text, a “spacecraft” is ___.
opts: a scientist who studies stars
a photo taken in space
a TV show about space
a machine that travels in space
q.why: spacecraft = 太空船；Voyager 1 是一艘太空船。

q.q: Why did Sagan think the photo was important?
opts: It proved Earth is the brightest planet
It was the first photo NASA ever took
It showed our planet is small and special, so we should care for it and each other
It helped NASA find new planets
q.why: 最後一段：our planet is small and special, so we must take care of it and of each other。

q.q: Your class is making a poster about the Pale Blue Dot. Which title fits Sagan's message best?
opts: “One Small Home — Let's Take Care of It Together”
“Earth: The Biggest Planet of All”
“How to Build a Spacecraft”
“Space Is Too Far to Matter”
q.why: 薩根想傳達地球渺小而珍貴，要彼此照顧；第二個標題最符合。

gt.en: He grew up to be a scientist who studied planets.
gt.zh: 他長大後成為一位研究行星的科學家。

gt.en: He also made a famous TV show called Cosmos.
gt.zh: 他也製作了一個有名的電視節目，叫做《宇宙》。

gt.en: In 1990, a spacecraft called Voyager 1 was very far from home.
gt.zh: 1990 年，一艘叫做航海家一號的太空船離家非常遙遠。

gt.en: Sagan asked NASA to turn its camera and take a photo of Earth.
gt.zh: 薩根請 NASA 把它的相機轉過來，拍一張地球的照片。

b.title: Seeing Ourselves from Six Billion Kilometres Away
text: Carl Sagan, born in New York on November 9, 1934, became one of the best-known scientists of the twentieth century — not only for his research on planets but for his gift for explaining science to ordinary people.
His 1980 television series Cosmos took viewers on a journey from atoms to galaxies and was watched by hundreds of millions of people around the world.

Sagan also helped plan NASA's missions to other planets. For the two Voyager spacecraft launched in 1977, he led the team that chose sounds, music and pictures for a golden record meant for any aliens who might find it.
In 1990, Voyager 1 was about six billion kilometres from Earth. At Sagan's urging, NASA turned the spacecraft around to photograph its home planet one last time.
In the image, Earth appears as a tiny, pale blue speck, smaller than a single pixel, floating in a beam of scattered sunlight.

Sagan argued that the photo should make us humble: every war, every empire and every person who ever lived existed on that tiny dot, which is all the more reason to treat it, and one another, with care.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Voyager 1 carried a golden record with sounds and music from Earth.
Carl Sagan made science popular and used a distant photo of Earth to remind people how small and precious our planet is.
Cosmos was watched by hundreds of millions of people around the world.
Sagan helped NASA plan missions to many other planets.
q.why: 其他三項都是文中的真實細節，但只有第二項涵蓋全文重點。

q.q: How far from Earth was Voyager 1 when it took the photo?
opts: About six million kilometres
About sixty billion kilometres
As far as the edge of our galaxy
About six billion kilometres
q.why: 第四段：about six billion kilometres from Earth。

q.q: What was the golden record for?
opts: To play music for astronauts during the long trip
To store the photos Voyager took
To carry sounds, music and pictures of Earth for any aliens who might find it
To record Cosmos for future viewers
q.why: 第三段：for a golden record meant for any aliens who might find it。

q.q: In paragraph 6, “humble” means ___.
opts: aware that you are not as important as you might think
proud of what humans have built
afraid of what might be in space
excited about future discoveries
q.why: humble = 謙卑的；照片讓人明白自己的渺小。

q.q: Why does the writer say Earth was “smaller than a single pixel”?
opts: To show how tiny Earth looks from that great distance
To suggest the camera was not working properly
To explain why scientists could not use the photo
To prove that Earth is smaller than other planets
q.why: 強調從那麼遠的地方看，地球小得連一個像素都不到。

q.q: Two countries are arguing about a small piece of land. Which sentence would Sagan most likely say to them?
opts: “The stronger country should take the land.”
“Space travel is more important than land.”
“Each country should build its own spacecraft.”
“From far away, all of us share one tiny planet — we should solve this with care.”
q.why: 第六段：每場戰爭、每個帝國都發生在那個小點上，所以要彼此善待——第二句最符合他的觀點。

tr.en: Sagan also helped plan NASA's missions to other planets.
tr.zh: 薩根也協助規劃 NASA 前往其他行星的任務。

tr.en: At Sagan's urging, NASA turned the spacecraft around to photograph its home planet one last time.
tr.zh: 在薩根的力勸下，NASA 把太空船轉過來，最後一次拍攝它的家鄉星球。

tr.en: In the image, Earth appears as a tiny, pale blue speck, smaller than a single pixel, floating in a beam of scattered sunlight.
tr.zh: 在影像中，地球看起來像一個微小的淡藍色小點，比一個像素還小，飄浮在一道散射的陽光裡。

c.title: The Smallest Photograph Ever Taken of Everything
text: Few scientists have been as comfortable in front of a camera as Carl Sagan. Born in Brooklyn on November 9, 1934, he combined serious planetary research with an almost evangelical conviction that science belonged to everyone, a belief he carried into the 1980 series Cosmos, which reached audiences of hundreds of millions.

His most enduring idea, however, came from a photograph that was nearly never taken. By 1990 Voyager 1 had completed its scientific tour of the outer planets and was heading out of the solar system. Pointing its camera back toward the Sun risked damaging the instruments, and some engineers saw little scientific value in the attempt.
Sagan persisted. The resulting image showed Earth from roughly six billion kilometres away as a fraction of a pixel, a pale blue mote caught in a streak of scattered light.

In his writing he turned that speck into a meditation on perspective: every quarrel and conquest in human history had played out on that minuscule stage, and no help, he observed, was likely to come from elsewhere to save us from ourselves.

The photograph is scientifically trivial and philosophically enormous — a reminder that sometimes the most important thing an instrument can show us is not something new, but ourselves, seen clearly for the first time.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's point?
opts: The Pale Blue Dot photo added important new scientific data about Earth.
A photo of little scientific value became a powerful lesson about humanity's place in the universe.
Sagan was more interested in television fame than in research.
Voyager 1's mission ended because the photo damaged its instruments.
q.why: 主旨：科學價值不大的照片，卻成為關於人類處境的強大啟示。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “persisted” means Sagan ___.
opts: kept pushing for the photo despite objections
quietly accepted the engineers' decision
changed the plan to photograph Mars instead
persuaded the engineers immediately
q.why: persisted = 堅持；即使有人反對仍堅持拍照。

q.q: Why did some engineers resist taking the photo?
opts: They thought Earth would look too dark to see
Voyager 1 had already run out of power
They wanted to save the camera for a future planet
Pointing the camera toward the Sun risked damage and seemed to offer little scientific value
q.why: 第二段：risked damaging the instruments … little scientific value。

q.q: How would you describe the writer's attitude toward the photo?
opts: Neutral and purely technical
Sceptical about its importance
Admiring and reflective
Nostalgic but disappointed
q.why: 作者稱它 philosophically enormous，語氣欽佩且深思。

q.q: What contrast does the final paragraph draw?
opts: Between Sagan's research and his television work
Between the photo's small scientific value and its large philosophical meaning
Between the engineers' fears and the photo's success
Between Earth and the other planets Voyager visited
q.why: 結尾：scientifically trivial and philosophically enormous。

q.q: A student says: “A photo with no new scientific data is a waste of money.” Which response best reflects the writer's view?
opts: Agree — science should only collect new data.
Agree — the engineers were right to resist.
Disagree — the photo actually contained a lot of new data.
Disagree — some images matter because they change how we see ourselves, not because they add data.
q.why: 作者認為照片的價值在於讓我們重新看見自己（結尾句），而非新數據。

discuss: If you could send one sound or picture from Earth to aliens, what would you choose and why?
Sagan believed science belongs to everyone. How can scientists make their work easier for ordinary people to understand?
Does seeing Earth as a tiny dot change how you think about arguments between people or countries? Explain.

topic: Sesame Street: How a TV Street Taught the World
zh: 芝麻街：一條教會全世界的電視街道
src: PBS · The New York Times · NBC

a.title: Can You Tell Me How to Get to Sesame Street?
text: On November 10, 1969, a new TV show started in the United States. It was called Sesame Street.
The show was made for young children. It taught letters, numbers, and how to be kind.
The show had funny puppets called Muppets, like Big Bird, Elmo, and Cookie Monster.
Children learned while they laughed. The songs were short and easy to remember.
Today, Sesame Street is shown in more than 150 countries. Some countries make their own version with new characters.
Many adults around the world first learned to count with Sesame Street.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The puppets on Sesame Street, like Big Bird and Elmo
How Sesame Street is made in more than 150 countries
A children's TV show that has helped kids around the world learn
Songs that help children remember numbers
q.why: 全文介紹《芝麻街》如何幫助孩子學習；布偶、各國版本、歌曲都是細節。

q.q: What did the show teach?
opts: Only songs and dances
How to make puppets
Letters and numbers, but not manners
Letters, numbers, and how to be kind
q.why: 第二段：letters, numbers, and how to be kind。

q.q: In how many countries is Sesame Street shown today?
opts: In more than 150 countries
Only in the United States
In about 15 countries
In every country in the world
q.why: 第五段：more than 150 countries。

q.q: In the text, “puppets” are ___.
opts: actors who wear animal costumes
toy figures that people move to make them act
cartoon drawings on TV
children who sing on the show
q.why: puppets = 布偶。

q.q: Why do some countries make their own version of the show?
opts: So the show fits their own children, language and culture
Because the American version was too expensive
Because children did not like Big Bird
So they can stop showing the American version
q.why: 各國用自己的角色和語言，讓節目更貼近當地孩子。

q.q: A little cousin finds counting boring. Based on the text, which idea would most likely help?
opts: Give the cousin a long list of numbers to copy
Use a short, funny song about counting
Tell the cousin to wait until school starts
Show a long lesson with no pictures
q.why: 第四段：孩子在歡笑中學習，短歌好記——用好玩的短歌最符合文章的方法。

gt.en: It taught letters, numbers, and how to be kind.
gt.zh: 它教字母、數字，還有如何待人親切。

gt.en: The show had funny puppets called Muppets, like Big Bird, Elmo, and Cookie Monster.
gt.zh: 這個節目有一些好笑的布偶，叫做布偶家族，像是大鳥、艾蒙和餅乾怪獸。

gt.en: The songs were short and easy to remember.
gt.zh: 這些歌又短又好記。

gt.en: Some countries make their own version with new characters.
gt.zh: 有些國家用新的角色製作自己的版本。

b.title: The Experiment That Became a Neighbourhood
text: When Sesame Street first aired on November 10, 1969, it was a bold experiment: could television, which many parents saw as a waste of time, actually help young children learn?
The idea came from television producer Joan Ganz Cooney and psychologist Lloyd Morrisett, who noticed that children from poorer families often started school behind their classmates.
Their team worked closely with educational researchers, testing each segment to see whether children paid attention and remembered what they had seen.
Jim Henson's Muppets made the lessons lively. Big Bird, Elmo and Cookie Monster became stars, and short, catchy songs turned the alphabet into something to sing.
The show also set its stories on a diverse city street where people of different backgrounds lived together, which was unusual for television at the time.
Over the decades, local versions have been produced around the world, each adapting the lessons to its own culture — proof that a good idea about learning can travel far.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Sesame Street was a carefully tested experiment that showed TV could help children learn, and it spread around the world.
Jim Henson's Muppets made Sesame Street popular all over the world.
Sesame Street was created because parents in 1969 loved television.
Sesame Street's street showed people of different backgrounds living together.
q.why: 其他選項是細節或與文意相反；第二項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Why did Cooney and Morrisett start the show?
opts: To give Jim Henson's Muppets their own TV show
Parents wanted more cartoons on TV
Schools asked for a show to replace teachers
Children from poorer families often started school behind their classmates
q.why: 第二段：children from poorer families often started school behind。

q.q: What was unusual about the show's street?
opts: It was filmed in a real neighbourhood in New York
Only puppets lived there, with no humans
People of different backgrounds lived together there
It changed to a new city every season
q.why: 第五段：a diverse city street where people of different backgrounds lived together。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “bold” means ___.
opts: carefully planned and safe
willing to take risks
very popular
expensive to make
q.why: bold = 大膽的。

q.q: Why did the team test each segment with children?
opts: To check whether children paid attention and learned from it
To choose which children could appear on TV
To find out which puppet was the most popular
To make sure the show was long enough
q.why: 第三段：testing each segment to see whether children paid attention and remembered。

q.q: Your school wants to make a short learning video for first graders. Which step follows the Sesame Street method most closely?
opts: Make the video as long as possible so it covers everything
Ask only teachers which songs they like
Copy a Sesame Street episode exactly
Show a draft to some first graders and change the parts they don't remember
q.why: 《芝麻街》的關鍵是「先給孩子看、測試、再修改」（第三段）。

tr.en: Their team worked closely with educational researchers, testing each segment to see whether children paid attention and remembered what they had seen.
tr.zh: 他們的團隊和教育研究人員密切合作，測試每一個片段，看看孩子們是否專心看，並記得看過的內容。

tr.en: Big Bird, Elmo and Cookie Monster became stars, and short, catchy songs turned the alphabet into something to sing.
tr.zh: 大鳥、艾蒙和餅乾怪獸都成了明星，簡短好記的歌曲讓字母變成可以唱的東西。

c.title: Teaching by Television
text: In 1969 the idea that television could educate small children struck many critics as faintly absurd. The medium was widely regarded as a 'vast wasteland', and few believed that a programme sandwiched between advertisements could teach anything worth knowing.

Sesame Street, which premiered on November 10 of that year, set out to prove them wrong — and, unusually, to measure whether it had. Producer Joan Ganz Cooney and psychologist Lloyd Morrisett built research into the production process itself, revising segments that failed to hold children's attention or to leave a trace in their memory.
The aim was explicitly social. Children from low-income homes were arriving at school already behind, and television reached them where books often did not.
Jim Henson's Muppets supplied the charm that made the method palatable, while the show's integrated street quietly modelled a society in which difference was ordinary.

Decades of studies have since associated the programme with gains in early literacy and numeracy, and its international co-productions have adapted its format to contexts from South Africa to the Middle East. Its legacy is less a set of characters than an argument: that entertainment and education need not be enemies if learning is designed, tested and taken seriously.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Sesame Street succeeded mainly because of its famous puppets.
Television in 1969 was mostly educational.
International versions are more successful than the original.
Sesame Street showed that entertainment can educate when learning is carefully designed and tested.
q.why: 主旨：只要學習經過設計與測試，娛樂也能教育。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “palatable” means ___.
opts: difficult but useful
pleasant or easy to accept
old-fashioned
expensive to produce
q.why: palatable = 容易接受的。

q.q: What made Sesame Street unusual compared with most TV shows of its time?
opts: It was paid for entirely by advertisements
It was the first show made for children
It used research to test and revise its content
It was filmed in many countries at once
q.why: 第二段：built research into the production process itself。

q.q: How does the writer present the 1969 critics?
opts: As people whose doubts the show set out to disprove
As experts who were later proven right
As the people who first suggested the show
As unfair enemies of children's education
q.why: set out to prove them wrong——作者把批評者當作被節目推翻的觀點。

q.q: What does the final sentence do?
opts: Summarises the show's most popular characters
Introduces criticism of the show
Describes the show's future plans
States the broader lesson of the show's legacy
q.why: 結尾總結：entertainment and education need not be enemies。

q.q: A parent says: “Any cartoon my child enjoys must be educational.” Based on the text, what is the best reply?
opts: “Not necessarily — enjoyment helps, but learning has to be designed and tested.”
“True — if children enjoy it, they learn from it.”
“True — that is exactly what the 1969 critics believed.”
“Not at all — entertainment can never teach anything.”
q.why: 作者主張娛樂與教育可以結合，但前提是學習經過設計與測試。

discuss: Did you learn anything from a TV show or video when you were small? What was it?
Can entertainment and learning go together? Give an example from your own life.
If you created a TV show to teach children in Taiwan, what would it teach and who would the characters be?

topic: Singles' Day: From a Joke to the World's Biggest Sale
zh: 雙十一：從玩笑變成全球最大購物節

a.title: Why 11/11 Is a Shopping Day
text: The date November 11 looks like four ones: 11/11. In China, some students called it Singles' Day, a day for people without a boyfriend or girlfriend.
At first, it was just a joke. Students had parties and bought small gifts for themselves.
In 2009, a big online shopping company started selling things at low prices on that day.
Soon, millions of people were shopping online on November 11. Now it is one of the biggest shopping days in the world.
In Taiwan, many online shops also have 11/11 sales.
But shopping too much is not always good. Some people buy things they do not need, and the boxes make a lot of waste.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why the date 11/11 looks like four ones
How online shops in Taiwan have 11/11 sales
How Singles' Day changed from a student joke into a huge shopping day
Why boxes from online shopping make a lot of waste
q.why: 全文講雙十一的轉變；其他是細節。

q.q: Why was the day first called Singles' Day?
opts: It was the day a shopping company was started
It is a holiday for students in China
Shops sold only one item that day
The date looks like four ones, like single people
q.why: 第一段：looks like four ones … a day for people without a boyfriend or girlfriend。

q.q: What happened in 2009?
opts: A big online shopping company started low-price sales on that day
Students had the first Singles' Day party
Taiwan started its first 11/11 sale
Singles' Day became a national holiday
q.why: 第三段：In 2009, a big online shopping company started selling things at low prices。

q.q: In the text, “waste” means ___.
opts: money that people save
things that are thrown away
things that are on sale
boxes that are reused
q.why: waste = 廢棄物。

q.q: What does the writer think about shopping on 11/11?
opts: Everyone should wait for 11/11 to buy things
It can be fun, but buying too much is not always good
It is only for students
It is bad, so no one should do it
q.why: 最後一段：shopping too much is not always good。

q.q: On 11/11 you see a sale on a game you don't really need. What would the writer most likely advise?
opts: Buy it quickly before the sale ends
Buy two so you can give one away
Think about whether you really need it before buying
Buy it because everyone else is buying things
q.why: 文章提醒有人買了不需要的東西——先想清楚是否需要。

gt.en: Students had parties and bought small gifts for themselves.
gt.zh: 學生們開派對，還買小禮物送給自己。

gt.en: In 2009, a big online shopping company started selling things at low prices on that day.
gt.zh: 2009 年，一家大型網路購物公司開始在那天低價賣東西。

gt.en: Soon, millions of people were shopping online on November 11.
gt.zh: 很快地，數百萬人在十一月十一日上網購物。

gt.en: In Taiwan, many online shops also have 11/11 sales.
gt.zh: 在台灣，許多網路商店也有雙十一特價。

b.title: How a Student Joke Became a Shopping Giant
text: Singles' Day began in the 1990s as a joke among university students in Nanjing, China. Because the date 11/11 is made up of four ones, they adopted it as a day to celebrate being single.
In 2009 the e-commerce company Alibaba saw a business opportunity and held a one-day online sale. Only a few dozen brands took part, but the idea caught on fast.

Within a decade, Singles' Day had grown into the world's largest shopping event, far bigger than America's Black Friday. Sales were counted live on giant screens, and in 2021 Alibaba reported orders worth over 80 billion US dollars during the festival period.
The event spread across Asia, including Taiwan, where online platforms now offer 11/11 discounts.
Its critics point to the costs. Mountains of packaging create waste, delivery vehicles add pollution, and clever marketing encourages impulse buying — purchases people later regret.
In recent years the festival has become quieter, as companies stopped announcing record totals and shoppers became more careful with money.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Singles' Day began as a student joke and grew into a giant shopping event, with both benefits and costs.
In 2021, Alibaba reported orders worth over 80 billion US dollars.
Singles' Day is now bigger than Black Friday in America.
Students in Nanjing chose 11/11 because it has four ones.
q.why: 只有第二項涵蓋起源、成長與代價。

q.q: How many brands took part in the first sale in 2009?
opts: A few hundred
Several thousand
Every brand in China
Only a few dozen
q.why: 第二段：Only a few dozen brands took part。

q.q: Which is NOT mentioned as a cost of the festival?
opts: Packaging waste
Shops closing because of low prices
Pollution from delivery vehicles
Impulse buying
q.why: 第五段列出包裝、汙染、衝動購物；沒有提到商店倒閉。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “impulse buying” means buying things ___.
opts: only after comparing many prices
in large amounts to save money
suddenly, without careful thought
for other people as gifts
q.why: impulse buying = 衝動購物。

q.q: What does the last paragraph suggest about the festival today?
opts: It is growing faster than ever
It has been replaced by Black Friday
It is now only for single people
It has become less showy as companies and shoppers changed
q.why: 最後一段：the festival has become quieter。

q.q: An online shop shows a countdown: “Only 5 minutes left! Buy now!” Based on the text, why might this be a problem?
opts: It creates pressure that can lead to impulse buying
It means the products are low quality
It makes delivery slower
It is against the law in Taiwan
q.why: 倒數製造急迫感，促成文章提到的衝動購物。

tr.en: Because the date 11/11 is made up of four ones, they adopted it as a day to celebrate being single.
tr.zh: 因為 11/11 這個日期是由四個一組成的，他們就把它當作慶祝單身的日子。

tr.en: In 2009 the e-commerce company Alibaba saw a business opportunity and held a one-day online sale.
tr.zh: 2009 年，電子商務公司阿里巴巴看到了商機，舉辦了一場為期一天的網路特賣。

tr.en: Mountains of packaging create waste, delivery vehicles add pollution, and clever marketing encourages impulse buying — purchases people later regret.
tr.zh: 堆積如山的包裝製造了垃圾，送貨車輛增加了汙染，而聰明的行銷手法則鼓勵衝動購物——也就是人們事後會後悔的購買。

c.title: The Business of Being Alone
text: Few commercial phenomena illustrate the inventiveness of modern marketing as neatly as Singles' Day. What began in the 1990s as a self-mocking ritual among Nanjing university students, who chose 11/11 for its four solitary ones, has been transformed into the largest retail event on the planet.

The pivotal moment came in 2009, when Alibaba repackaged the date as an online sale. The company understood that a festival without traditions could be filled with whatever meaning sold best, and it supplied gala shows, countdowns and real-time sales tallies that turned shopping into a spectator sport.
By 2021 the reported value of orders exceeded 80 billion US dollars, dwarfing America's Black Friday.

Success, however, attracted scrutiny. Environmental groups highlighted the packaging generated by billions of parcels, economists noted how artificial urgency fuels impulsive spending, and regulators grew wary of the platforms' power.

Since then the event has grown more subdued; companies stopped trumpeting record totals and consumers have become more frugal. Singles' Day thus offers a compact lesson in how a date can be manufactured into a festival — and how the meaning a market creates can also, gradually, be questioned.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Singles' Day is an ancient Chinese tradition that Alibaba revived.
Singles' Day shows how marketing can turn a date into a huge festival, and how that meaning can later be questioned.
Online shopping festivals are harmful and should be banned.
Singles' Day became popular because single people are lonely.
q.why: 主旨：行銷能把日期打造成節慶，這種意義也可能被質疑。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “frugal” means ___.
opts: careful not to spend much money
eager to buy new things
suspicious of companies
loyal to one brand
q.why: frugal = 節儉的。

q.q: Why does the writer say a festival “without traditions could be filled with whatever meaning sold best”?
opts: Because traditional festivals are not allowed to have sales
Because students had already planned the meaning
Because the government chose the meaning
Because a new festival had no fixed meaning, so a company could shape it to encourage buying
q.why: 第二段：沒有傳統包袱的節日，可以被填入最好賣的意義。

q.q: How does the writer view Singles' Day?
opts: Enthusiastic — it is a model for every country
Hostile — it is purely harmful
Analytical — impressed by its inventiveness but aware of its costs
Neutral — the writer gives no opinion
q.why: 既讚嘆行銷創意，也指出環境與消費問題。

q.q: How is the essay organised?
opts: Problem → solution → result
A comparison of Singles' Day and Black Friday throughout
Origin → commercial transformation → scale → criticism → recent change and lesson
Criticism first, then the history
q.why: 結構：起源 → 商業化 → 規模 → 批評 → 近年變化與啟示。

q.q: Which modern example is MOST similar to how Singles' Day was created?
opts: A traditional festival that families have celebrated for centuries
A company inventing “Pet Love Day” with discounts on pet products
A national holiday chosen to remember a war
A school sports day planned by students
q.why: 雙十一是企業把一個日期包裝成購物節；公司自創節日促銷最相似。

discuss: Have you or your family ever bought something on 11/11? Was it something you really needed?
How can shoppers avoid impulse buying when there are big sales?
Do you think online shopping festivals are good or bad for the environment? What could companies do better?

a.title: A City Cut into the Rocks
text: Petra is an old city in the desert of Jordan. Its buildings are not built with bricks. They are cut into the pink and red rocks!
People called the Nabataeans made the city more than 2,000 years ago.
To enter Petra, you walk through a long, narrow path between high rocks. It is called the Siq.
At the end of the path, you see a beautiful building called the Treasury. It is very tall.
The Nabataeans were clever with water. They made channels to catch rain in the dry desert.
Today, many tourists visit Petra. Some ride camels or donkeys to see more of the old city.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?

An ancient city carved into rocks in Jordan
How the Nabataeans collected rain
Tourists riding camels in the desert

q.q: What is the Siq?

A channel that carries rainwater
The name of the people who built Petra
A long, narrow path between high rocks

They dug deep wells under the Treasury

very long

Visit the water channels on the top of the Treasury

gt.zh: 要進入佩特拉，你得走過一條夾在高聳岩石之間、又長又窄的小路。

gt.zh: 納巴泰人很懂得運用水。

b.title: Hidden City of the Desert
text: Hidden among the mountains of southern Jordan, Petra is one of the most astonishing archaeological sites on Earth. Its temples and tombs were carved directly into rose-coloured sandstone cliffs.
The city was the capital of the Nabataeans, Arab traders who grew wealthy by controlling caravan routes that carried incense and spices across the desert more than two thousand years ago.

Visitors enter through the Siq, a winding canyon about a kilometre long whose walls rise as high as 80 metres. At its end, the facade of Al-Khazneh, known as the Treasury, suddenly appears in the sunlight.
Despite the dry climate, the Nabataeans supported a large population by building dams, cisterns and channels to collect and store rainwater.

After trade routes shifted and earthquakes struck, Petra slowly declined. For centuries it was known mainly to local Bedouin, until a Swiss traveller, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, described it to Europeans in 1812.
Today Petra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Jordan works to balance tourism with the need to protect the fragile stone.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The Treasury is a famous building carved into the cliffs of Petra.
Burckhardt was the first person ever to find Petra.
The Nabataeans grew rich by trading incense and spices.
Petra, an ancient trading capital carved into stone, is now a protected world treasure.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是部分細節或錯誤說法。

q.q: How did the Nabataeans become wealthy?
opts: By controlling caravan routes for incense and spices
By selling the rose-coloured stone
By charging tourists to enter the Siq
By farming the desert with rainwater
q.why: 第二段：controlling caravan routes that carried incense and spices。

q.q: Why did Petra decline?
opts: The water channels dried up suddenly
Burckhardt took its treasures to Europe
Trade routes shifted and earthquakes struck
Too many tourists damaged it
q.why: 第五段：After trade routes shifted and earthquakes struck。

q.q: In paragraph 3, a “canyon” is ___.
opts: a wide, flat desert
a deep, narrow valley with steep sides
a carved stone building
a road built by traders
q.why: canyon = 峽谷。

q.q: What does the writer suggest by saying Petra was known mainly to local Bedouin?

It was not truly lost; Burckhardt made it known to Europeans
No one lived near Petra for centuries
The Bedouin kept it secret from Burckhardt
q.why: 當地人一直知道它，布克哈特是讓歐洲人知道。

q.q: Which plan best matches the text's idea of balancing tourism and protection at Petra?

Allow unlimited visitors because tourism brings money

Rebuild the old buildings with new stone
q.why: 最後一段：balance tourism with the need to protect the fragile stone——限制人數、固定路線最平衡。

tr.en: Hidden among the mountains of southern Jordan, Petra is one of the most astonishing archaeological sites on Earth.
tr.zh: 隱藏在約旦南部群山之間的佩特拉，是地球上最令人驚嘆的考古遺址之一。

tr.en: Visitors enter through the Siq, a winding canyon about a kilometre long whose walls rise as high as 80 metres.
tr.zh: 遊客從「蛇道」進入，這是一條大約一公里長的蜿蜒峽谷，兩側的岩壁高達八十公尺。

tr.en: After trade routes shifted and earthquakes struck, Petra slowly declined.
tr.zh: 在貿易路線改變、又遭遇地震之後，佩特拉慢慢地衰落了。

c.title: Wealth Carved in Stone
text: Petra is often described as a lost city, but its real story is one of calculated prosperity. Carved into the rose-red sandstone of southern Jordan, it served as the capital of the Nabataeans, who grew rich by taxing and protecting the caravans that carried incense, myrrh and spices between Arabia and the Mediterranean.

The approach is pure theatre. Visitors thread their way through the Siq, a narrow gorge whose walls tower above them, until the facade of Al-Khazneh, the so-called Treasury, bursts into view, its columns cut, not built, from the living rock.

Less photogenic but more remarkable was the city's hydraulic engineering. In an arid landscape, the Nabataeans built dams, terracotta pipes and cisterns that captured flash floods and sustained a population of perhaps tens of thousands.

Petra's decline was gradual rather than sudden: Roman annexation, shifting trade routes toward the sea and devastating earthquakes eroded its importance until only Bedouin herders remained to know it.

Today, its popularity poses a quieter threat. Salt, wind and millions of footsteps wear at the soft stone, and conservationists argue that preserving Petra requires limiting the very admiration that keeps it famous.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Petra was suddenly destroyed by one great earthquake.
Petra's most important feature is the Treasury's facade.
Petra's story is one of clever prosperity and slow decline, and today its fame itself threatens it.
Petra survived because no one ever visited it.
q.why: 主旨：精明的繁榮與緩慢衰落，如今名氣本身成為威脅。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “arid” means ___.

very rocky

q.q: Why does the writer call Petra's water system “more remarkable” than the Treasury?

Tourists prefer to visit the water system

q.why: 第三段：在乾旱地區養活大量人口，比華麗外觀更了不起。

q.q: How does the writer describe the entrance through the Siq?

As dramatic, like theatre

q.why: 第二段：The approach is pure theatre。

q.q: What irony does the final paragraph point out?

Protecting Petra may require limiting the admiration that keeps it famous

q.why: 結尾：preserving Petra requires limiting the very admiration that keeps it famous。

q.q: Which piece of evidence would BEST support the writer's claim that popularity threatens Petra?
opts: A record of how many camels live near Petra

a.title: Small Acts, Big Smiles
text: November 13 is World Kindness Day. It is a day to be kind to others.
Kindness can be very simple. You can smile at someone, help a classmate, or say thank you.
You can hold the door for someone, or share your snack with a friend.
When you are kind, other people feel happy. Scientists say it can make you feel happy too!

What kind thing can you do today?

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How scientists study happiness
World Kindness Day and simple ways to be kind
How to share snacks with friends
Why people should always hold the door

To make readers think about doing something kind

b.title: Why Kindness Is Contagious
text: World Kindness Day, held every November 13, was introduced in 1998 by the World Kindness Movement, a group that grew out of a conference in Tokyo the year before.
The idea is simple: to encourage people everywhere to notice others and do something good for them, without expecting anything back.

Research suggests that kindness benefits the giver as well as the receiver. Studies have found that people who spend money or time on others often report feeling happier than those who spend it only on themselves.
Kindness also appears to be contagious. In experiments, people who received help were more likely to help someone else later, creating a chain of generosity.
Small acts count. Including a lonely classmate, writing a thank-you note or simply listening carefully can change someone's day.
Of course, kindness is not the same as always saying yes. Being kind sometimes means being honest or standing up for someone who is being treated unfairly.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: World Kindness Day started at a conference in Tokyo.
Kind people should always say yes to others.
Spending money on others is the best way to be happy.
Kindness helps both the giver and the receiver and can spread from person to person.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第二項是細節；第三、四項與文意不符或太絕對。

q.q: Where did the World Kindness Movement grow out of?
opts: A school project in Taiwan
A science study in America
A conference in Tokyo
A UN meeting in 1998
q.why: 第一段：grew out of a conference in Tokyo。

q.q: What did experiments show about people who received help?
opts: They felt they had to pay the helper back
They were more likely to help someone else later
They became less independent
They forgot the help quickly
q.why: 第四段：more likely to help someone else later。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “contagious” means ___.
opts: able to spread from one person to another
harmful to your health
easy to forget
only shared with friends
q.why: contagious = 會傳染的。

q.q: What does the last paragraph suggest?
opts: Kind people should avoid disagreeing
Real kindness can include honesty and standing up for others
Kindness means doing whatever others ask
Being honest is less important than being nice
q.why: 最後一段：Being kind sometimes means being honest or standing up for someone。

q.q: A classmate is being laughed at by a group. According to the text, which action is the kindest?
opts: Laugh a little so the group doesn't target you
Ignore it because it is not your problem

tr.en: The idea is simple: to encourage people everywhere to notice others and do something good for them, without expecting anything back.
tr.zh: 這個想法很簡單：鼓勵各地的人留意身邊的人，為他們做點好事，而且不求回報。

tr.en: Research suggests that kindness benefits the giver as well as the receiver.
tr.zh: 研究顯示，善意不只對接受的人有好處，對付出的人也有好處。

tr.en: In experiments, people who received help were more likely to help someone else later, creating a chain of generosity.
tr.zh: 在實驗中，得到幫助的人後來比較可能去幫助別人，形成一條慷慨的連鎖。

c.title: The Quiet Economics of Kindness
text: Kindness is easy to dismiss as sentimental, a soft virtue for greeting cards. World Kindness Day, observed every November 13 since the World Kindness Movement proposed it in 1998, invites a more serious look.

Behavioural research has repeatedly found that prosocial spending — devoting money or time to others — is associated with greater wellbeing than equivalent spending on oneself. The effect appears across very different cultures, which suggests it is not merely a local custom.

Kindness also seems to propagate. Experiments on 'paying it forward' show that recipients of generosity are more inclined to extend it to strangers, so that a single act can ripple outward through a network of people who never meet.
None of this makes kindness simple. Genuine kindness can demand courage: telling an uncomfortable truth, refusing to join in mockery, or defending someone whom the group has decided to exclude.
Seen this way, kindness is less a mood than a practice — an everyday choice that, multiplied across a community, quietly shapes whether people feel safe enough to trust one another.

q.q: Why does the writer mention that the effect appears across different cultures?

To explain where the World Kindness Movement began

q.q: How does the writer treat the view that kindness is “sentimental”?

q.why: 結尾：kindness is less a mood than a practice。

q.q: A school wants to measure whether a “Kindness Week” worked. Which measure fits the writer's view best?
